title: Didn't want to shoot teen but had no choice, officer tells Winnipeg inquest
article: The Winnipeg police officer who shot and killed Matthew Dumas on a January afternoon in 2005 says the incident has haunted him ever since.

But Constable Dennis Gburek adds he had no other choice, as the 18-year-old Mr. Dumas continued to advance on him despite repeated warnings to drop a screwdriver, and despite having been pepper-sprayed twice by another officer.
"I'm yelling 'I'm going to shoot you,' he just keeps coming," Constable Gburek told a coroner's inquest yesterday.
The shooting prompted cries of racism from some aboriginal leaders, despite the fact Constable Gburek himself is Métis.
They said Mr. Dumas was just one of many young aboriginals targeted by police because of their skin colour.
The incident started when police responded to reports of a robbery and break-in in Winnipeg's north end - a crime that it turned out Mr. Dumas had nothing to do with.
Constable Gburek said he had stopped another young man a block away when he saw Mr. Dumas and another officer wrestling.
The other officer, Detective Jon Mateychuk, earlier testified he came across Mr. Dumas and tried to stop him, but Mr. Dumas ran. Det. Mateychuk eventually caught up with him and a struggle ensued.

Constable Gburek told the inquest he let his suspect go, started running toward the fight and got his baton out. When he saw Mr. Dumas had a weapon in his hand, he put away his baton and drew his gun.
"I'm yelling, 'Winnipeg police. Stop, police,' " he told the inquest.
It was then that Mr. Dumas started toward him, and he started backing up.
"His eyes are big, they're lit up. You can see the anger in him. He's showing his teeth," Constable Gburek said.
Det. Mateychuk used pepper spray on Mr. Dumas, hitting him mostly on the side of the head.

"He never even blocked his eyes, he looked right at me," Constable Gburek said. "I didn't want to shoot him. I didn't want to pull the trigger. I see [Mr. Dumas's] sweater and it's right over top of me and I think, 'Just shoot, just shoot.' "

Other witnesses have confirmed that Mr. Dumas ignored orders to drop his screwdriver. Some have questioned whether police could have tackled Mr. Dumas or used some other non-lethal means of controlling him, but Constable Gburek said police are trained to shoot armed persons who get within seven metres and continue with threatening advances.
Mr. Dumas was less than two metres away when Constable Gburek said he fired two shots into the centre of his body.
The lawyer for the Dumas family, Donald Worme, has suggested police could have used a baton to subdue Mr. Dumas.
He also accused Det. Mateychuk of missing a chance to end the standoff before it became deadly.

He suggested yesterday Constable Gburek could have continued to back away from Mr. Dumas instead of firing his weapon, because there was break between a chain-link fence and a large snowbank on either side of the officer.
"There was another option," Mr. Worme said.
Constable Gburek replied that he had no choice - that Mr. Dumas was by then close enough to stab him if he tried to turn and run.
Coroner's inquests are mandatory in Manitoba whenever the death involves a police shooting or someone in custody.
The shooting was the first time Constable Gburek had fired his weapon in the line of duty, after three years on the job. It continues to take an emotional toll, he told the inquest.
"I'm stressed to the max for the last three years, not sleeping, night sweats."
